https://aeon.co/essays/how-should-you-ch.question: How do we choose when several morally legitimate claims compete?
https://aeon.co/essays/how-should-you-ch.thesis: Moral life often requires allocating finite resources among competing goods, not merely defeating selfish impulses.
https://aeon.co/essays/how-should-you-ch.argument: First, individuals have multiple valuable commitments. Second, those commitments can conflict even when none is wrong. Third, isolated rules cannot determine how a life should be shaped. Therefore reflection on virtues, relationships and exemplary lives can help organize priorities.
https://aeon.co/essays/how-should-you-ch.intellectual_background: McMullin draws on virtue ethics and existentialist approaches to lived commitments and flourishing.
https://aeon.co/essays/how-should-you-ch.example: Time spent caring for a parent may conflict with a professional duty or an obligation to one's children; neither concern is automatically illegitimate.
https://aeon.co/essays/how-should-you-ch.strongest_objection: Role models and whole-life judgments can reflect privilege, prejudice or culturally narrow ideals, leaving immediate duties underspecified.
https://aeon.co/essays/how-should-you-ch.possible_response: Compare multiple exemplars, examine the concrete claims of those affected and make the tradeoff accountable rather than assuming any single life is ideal.
https://aeon.co/essays/how-should-you-ch.implications: Ethical maturity includes making defensible sacrifices among goods rather than imagining every good can be maximized.
